design_detail: Descriptive laboratory analysis of product samples, with no comparison group. The Wadsworth Center (the New York State Department of Health public health laboratory) analysed 38 samples of residual fluid from vaporizer cartridges recovered from the first 10 New York State patients with e-cigarette, or vaping, product use-associated lung injury (EVALI) for whom cartridges were obtained (the laboratory began receiving cartridges in August 2019), and six commercial products sold online as cannabis-oil diluents or thickeners. Untargeted screening by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) and high-resolution liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-HRMS/MS), then targeted measurement of 11 natural cannabinoids (HPLC with photodiode array), five mycotoxins, vitamin E acetate (VEA; GC-MS), the fungicide myclobutanil and the pesticide synergist piperonyl butoxide (PBO; LC-MS/MS), a screen of 884 pesticides and metabolites, and a screen for synthetic cannabinoids and 150 synthetic opioid compounds; nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) for the commercial products. Results are counts and percentages by mass; no statistical tests or intervals are given. Version read: the PMC full text of the Toxics article (2020;8(1):8).
can_establish: What was in the residual fluid of vaporizer cartridges recovered from 10 New York patients with EVALI in 2019: of 36 cannabinoid-containing fluids, 23 (64%) contained VEA, at 16 to 58% by mass; 14 or 15 contained medium-chain triglyceride (MCT) oil; most also held pesticide residues; some had unusually high delta-8-THC; none had synthetic cannabinoids, opioids or mycotoxins above the stated limits. It also shows that three of six commercial products sold online as cannabis-oil diluents or thickeners were essentially pure VEA, so VEA was on sale for this use.
cannot_establish: That VEA, or any other substance in the fluid, caused the lung injury: there are no fluids from people who vaped without injury, no dose or timing data and no result per patient. It cannot show what share of the 10 patients had a VEA-containing cartridge (13 of the 36 fluids had none), how common VEA was in cartridges in general in 2019, what the patients inhaled other than the residue left in the cartridge, or how these cartridges differ from legally sold ones (that contrast rests on the laboratory's earlier work with New York medical products, not on data shown here). The aerosol was not analysed; products formed when VEA is heated are mentioned from initial experiments that are not shown.

sample.recruitment: Cartridges and devices were obtained through New York Poison Control Centers and health care providers. Medical staff of the Department of Health's Center for Environmental Health reviewed each reported case's medical record for consistency with the CDC clinical description of EVALI; when case-associated cartridges were available they were sent to the Wadsworth Center (Methods 2.1). The six commercial products were bought on the internet by the Department of Health (Results 3.4).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Fluids from the first 10 New York EVALI cases for which cartridges were obtained. Cartridges with little fluid were centrifuged to recover it and run at adjusted dilution; sample 38 had too little material for the PBO test (Table 2). Whether any cartridge was excluded is not stated. How each cartridge was judged to be illicit is not described: the Methods call them case-associated and say that packing and markings were noted, but report neither.
sample.demographics: Not reported for the 10 patients (no age, sex, dates or hospital course). The only patient information is that, of the first 10 cases who provided product-use histories (the number who provided one is not stated), all reported using cannabinoid-containing vaping products and 80% reported using both cannabinoid- and nicotine-containing products (Discussion 4.3, 1st paragraph).
sample.attrition: Not applicable. Thirty-eight samples are analysed from 10 patients, about 3.8 per patient on average; the number per patient is not given.
sample.selection_effects: Only cartridges that patients, families or clinicians handed over, from 10 patients in one state, are analysed; who handed over cartridges and who did not is not described. The fluid is what was left in the cartridge at recovery, which may differ from what was inhaled earlier. No sample of cartridges from the wider market was taken, so the shares apply to these cartridges, not to cartridges in general.

exposure.measurement: Laboratory analysis of residual fluid, about 10 mg weighed into acetonitrile. VEA: GC-MS with a deuterated internal standard, calibration 0.039 to 2.5 micrograms per mL, analytical range 1 to 100% by mass; identity confirmed against an analytical standard by retention time, library mass spectrum and accurate mass (Results 3.1). Cannabinoids: HPLC with photodiode array, the method the laboratory has used for New York medical marijuana products since December 2015. MCT oil was estimated roughly (3 to 24% by mass) by comparing four peak areas with a commercial MCT oil, because standards for the individual components are not available. Pesticides: myclobutanil and PBO by LC-MS/MS; a wider screen with a cut-off of 1 microgram per gram. Synthetic cannabinoids and opioids: detection to 0.05% by mass.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not measured. The paper gives no information on how much each patient vaped, for how long, which cartridge they used when, or how the cartridges were obtained. The statement that vaping heats fluids to 250 to 350 degrees Celsius is made without a source.
exposure.polysubstance: Two of the 38 fluids held nicotine and no cannabinoids (samples 4 and 16); 36 held cannabinoids. Of the first 10 cases who provided product-use histories, 80% reported using both cannabinoid- and nicotine-containing vaping products.

comparison.controls: None within the study. The authors contrast the fluids with vaporizer products of New York State's medical marijuana program that the same laboratory has tested ('thousands of samples'): free of additives and 80 to 90% total cannabinoids (Discussion 4.1, 2nd paragraph). No data from those products are shown here. No fluids from people who vaped without injury, and none from legal retail in 2019, are analysed.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Which cartridge each patient used and when; how many cartridges each of the 10 patients contributed; where and how each was obtained; whether patients whose cartridges held no VEA (13 of 36 fluids) also used a cartridge that did.

outcomes.instruments: GC-MS and LC-HRMS/MS untargeted screens; HPLC with photodiode array for 11 natural cannabinoids; LC-MS/MS for five mycotoxins (aflatoxins B1, B2, G1, G2 and ochratoxin A), myclobutanil and PBO; GC-MS for VEA; Q-Orbitrap screen of 884 pesticides and metabolites; NMR, GC-MS and LC-HRMS/MS for the six commercial products.
outcomes.validity_norms: The cannabinoid, mycotoxin, myclobutanil and PBO methods are ones the New York laboratory has validated and had certified or accredited for medical marijuana products; they were adapted here (a scaled-down mycotoxin extraction because of small samples; cannabinoid samples run without the usual surrogate spike). The VEA method was developed for this work. Whether the methods perform the same in illicit fluids was not tested in the text read. Figures S1 to S6 and Table S1 (supplement) were not opened.
outcomes.operationalization: VEA 'found' means measured at 1% by mass or more; lower values are printed as below 1.0. A fluid is cannabinoid-containing if any of the 11 natural cannabinoids was quantified. The paper's 64% is 23 of 36 cannabinoid-containing fluids, not 23 of 38 fluids and not a share of patients.

analysis.effect_sizes: Cannabinoid-containing fluids (36): VEA in 23 (64%), 16.4 to 57.6% by mass, median 38.4% among the 23 (editors' calculation from Table 1); no detectable VEA in 13, of which 12 held MCT oil. MCT oil: 15 in the text, 14 marked in Table 1 (editors' count); both VEA and MCT in 2 fluids (samples 7 and 14); neither in 1 (sample 27). Delta-9-THC 3.1 to 66.3% by mass, median 29.6%; sum of quantified cannabinoids 23 to 73%, under 50% in 27 of 36 (editors' calculation; the paper gives no totals). Delta-8-THC quantified in 8, higher than delta-9-THC in 6 of them (editors' count). At least one pesticide (myclobutanil in 22, PBO in 18, other pesticides above 1 microgram per gram in 26 fluids) in 31 of the 36 (editors' count from Table 2); none in the other 5. Mycotoxins below 4.8 ng/g and synthetic cannabinoids and opioids below 0.05% by mass in all 38. Commercial products: three of six (two diluents, one thickener) essentially pure VEA, two squalane-based, one alpha-bisabolol-based. Update to 12 December 2019 given in the Conclusions without methods: 206 fluids from 61 New York cases, 147 containing THC and 59 nicotine; 101 of the 147 (69%) contained VEA. Editors' calculation, exact binomial 95% intervals, treating fluids as independent (they come from 10 and 61 patients, so these are too narrow): 23 of 36, 46% to 79%; 101 of 147, 61% to 76%.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not registered; a public health laboratory response analysed as samples arrived. The paper says the laboratory had no prior expectation of what the cartridges held (Results 3.1).
analysis.selective_reporting: All 38 samples are shown in Tables 1 and 2 and the six commercial products in Table 3. The untargeted screens are reported only for the additives and contaminants the authors discuss; other compounds seen are not tabulated in the text read. The extended series (206 fluids) and the heating experiments are reported as statements with no data.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among 36 cannabinoid-containing fluids recovered from 10 New York patients with EVALI, 23 (64%) held VEA at 16 to 58% by mass, 13 held none, 14 or 15 held MCT oil, 31 held at least one pesticide, and no synthetic cannabinoids, opioids or mycotoxins were found; cannabinoid content was mostly under 50% by mass; three of six commercial diluent and thickener products were essentially pure VEA.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title names VEA as a major diluent, and the abstract says the cause of EVALI is unknown. The Discussion says it is possible that VEA is causative or contributes, offers lipoid pneumonia and heating products as mechanisms, and states that there is no evidence that vaping large amounts of VEA, squalane or other diluents is safe. The Conclusions add that there is additional evidence of a strong association of VEA with EVALI (101 of 147 fluids and 28 of 28 lung-fluid samples in a CDC report) and that in vitro and in vivo studies will be required to establish cause. Gaps: (1) this paper has no comparison fluids, so the association is not tested within it; (2) 13 of 36 fluids held no VEA; (3) the contrast with legal products rests on unpublished laboratory experience; (4) the market timeline for VEA diluents (introduced in 2018, sales up in spring 2019) is sourced to trade-press articles on a cannabis-industry website, not peer-reviewed work; (5) heating products of VEA and the claim that pesticide contamination is 'intermittent and random' are inferences without data shown.

timeline.event: The laboratory shared its VEA findings with CDC, FDA and state health officials on 19 August and the New York State Department of Health announced them on 5 September (the authors' account; the announcement was not read).

The authors cite the FDA, Utah and Minnesota as later finding VEA in case-associated fluids; Blount et al. quote FDA testing that found it in 49% of case-associated THC product samples. These reports were not read; the proportions differ from this study's 64% and from the New York update's 69%.
CDC reported vitamin E acetate in lung fluid from 48 of 51 patients with EVALI and in none of 99 healthy volunteers (the New York laboratory cites an earlier CDC report of 28 of 28).
CDC update on the outbreak: 2,668 hospitalized patients by 14 January 2020, most who reported product use having used THC-containing products.

replication.where_it_stands: Several agencies are cited as finding VEA in case-associated products or lung fluid, and the New York figures overlap one another, so they are not independent replications. The proportions differ between reports. Whether VEA alone causes the injury is stated by the authors to need laboratory and animal studies.

funding.funder: This research received no external funding (Funding section).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no financial or other conflicts of interest (Conflicts of Interest section).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors work at the Wadsworth Center and the Center for Environmental Health of the New York State Department of Health, the University at Albany School of Public Health and Albany Medical Center. The Wadsworth laboratory also tests the state's medical marijuana products, which the paper uses as the comparison for the illicit fluids. A government health laboratory, not the cannabis or tobacco industry; no industry tie is declared.

what_would_settle_it: Testing every cartridge each patient used, by laboratories blind to case status, alongside cartridges from people of similar age and product use who vaped without injury and from legal retail in the same months, with the number of cartridges per patient and their source reported; plus experiments on the aerosol of VEA, with and without THC, at realistic temperatures.

domains.domain: Selection and provenance of the samples
domains.note: Cartridges from 10 patients in one state, handed over for analysis; the number per patient, the dates, the source of each cartridge and the basis for calling them illicit are not reported.

Mass-spectrometric identification confirmed against standards, validated or certified methods for most analytes, and detection limits stated. MCT oil is only roughly estimated, the VEA method is new, performance in this fluid type was not tested in the text read, and the supplement was not opened.

No fluids from people who vaped without injury or from legal retail; the contrast with New York medical products is the laboratory's experience and is not shown. The share with VEA cannot be read as higher or lower than other cartridges.

domains.domain: Link between the analysed product and the patient's illness
domains.note: Results are not given per patient; 13 of 36 fluids held no VEA; the residue in a recovered cartridge may not be what a patient inhaled earlier.

domains.domain: Separation of findings from inference about cause
domains.note: The findings are described as findings and cause is called unknown, but the Discussion's mechanisms, the safety statement about large amounts, the market timeline from trade press and the 'strong association' wording go beyond the data shown.

The text counts 15 fluids with MCT oil where Table 1 marks 14; the VEA ceiling is 57% in the Results, 57.6% in Table 1 and 58% in the Discussion; the extended series of 206 fluids has no methods or table; no per-sample MCT amounts are given.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a laboratory analysis of case-associated products (METHODS 5.3); the editors' checklist is used, with domains chosen for product analysis. The overall judgment is no milder than the worst domain. The chemistry is careful and the findings are clearly tabulated, and the authors keep the cause open. The paper may be cited for what was in the fluid of 38 cartridges recovered from 10 New York patients, for the VEA content of three commercial diluent and thickener products, and for the absence of the named synthetic compounds and mycotoxins. It may not be cited for the cause of EVALI, for how common VEA was in cartridges in general, for a difference from legal products, or for what any patient inhaled.

key_findings.finding: Thirty-eight samples of fluid from vaporizer cartridges recovered from the first 10 New York State patients with EVALI for whom cartridges were obtained were analysed; two held nicotine and no cannabinoids (samples 4 and 16) and 36 held cannabinoids. The laboratory began receiving cartridges in August 2019 and chose untargeted analysis because it had no prior information on what they held.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Introduction, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Results 3.2, 3rd paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: VEA was found in 23 of the 36 cannabinoid-containing fluids (64%), at 16 to 57% by mass (Table 1 maximum 57.6%; the Discussion says as much as 58%); 13 held none above 1% by mass. Editors' calculation: exact 95% interval 46% to 79%, treating the 36 fluids as independent, which they are not.
key_findings.locator: Results 3.2, 3rd paragraph; Table 1 (VEA column); Discussion 4.1, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: MCT oil was estimated at 3 to 24% by mass in the 15 fluids the text says held it (Table 1 marks 14 with a plus sign, by the editors' count); 12 of the 13 fluids without VEA held MCT oil and 2 held both. MCT was estimated roughly because standards for its components are not available.

Cannabinoid content was lower than the laboratory's usual medical products: delta-9-THC 3.1 to 66.3% by mass (median 29.6%, editors' calculation) in the 36; the authors say illicit fluids are usually under 50% cannabinoids against 80 to 90% in New York's medical program products (27 of 36 under 50% by the editors' sum of the quantified cannabinoids). Delta-8-THC was quantified in 8 fluids and exceeded delta-9-THC in 6 of them (editors' count).
key_findings.locator: Results 3.2, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Table 1; Discussion 4.1, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: The medical-program comparison is the laboratory's account; no data are shown. Table 1 units are not printed in the text read; per cent by mass is taken from the surrounding text.

key_findings.finding: Pesticides: myclobutanil was quantified in 22 fluids (up to 28.3 micrograms per gram), PBO in 18 (up to 24.1), and several other fungicides, insecticides and acaricides above 1 microgram per gram in 26; 31 of the 36 cannabinoid-containing fluids held at least one (editors' count). The authors judge the pattern intermittent and say EVALI is not due to a single pesticide. No mycotoxins (below 4.8 ng/g) and no synthetic cannabinoids or opioids (below 0.05% by mass) in any fluid.
key_findings.locator: Results 3.1, 5th paragraph; Results 3.3; Table 2; Discussion 4.1, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Of six commercial products bought online as cannabis-oil diluents or thickeners, two diluents and one thickener were essentially pure VEA, one diluent was mostly squalane with MCT and triethyl citrate, one thickener was squalane, and one thickener was alpha-bisabolol with a little isophytol. The sellers did not list ingredients on label or website.

Of the first 10 New York cases who provided product-use histories (number not stated), all reported using cannabinoid-containing vaping products and 80% reported using both cannabinoid- and nicotine-containing vaping products. The two nicotine-containing fluids held no unusual compounds of concern.

Update to 12 December 2019 (Conclusions, no methods or table): 206 fluids from 61 New York cases, 147 with THC and 59 with nicotine; 101 of 147 THC-containing fluids (69%) held VEA. Editors' calculation, exact 95% interval 61% to 76%, treating fluids as independent. The authors also cite 28 of 28 lung-fluid samples with VEA in an early CDC report, and CDC counts of 2,409 hospitalized cases and 52 deaths as of 12 December 2019, and 205 New York cases including 2 deaths as of 10 December.
key_findings.note: National and lung-fluid figures are the authors' citations of a CDC web page and an MMWR report, not read here.

key_findings.finding: The authors' timeline for the diluents rests on articles from a cannabis-industry news site: VEA-based diluents appeared on the market in 2018, sales greatly increased in spring 2019, and they were touted as tasteless, odourless and miscible with cannabis oil in all proportions. The authors also say cutting product with cheaper material the customer cannot detect is long-standing practice in illegal drug markets.
key_findings.note: Trade-press sources, not peer-reviewed; not read.

key_findings.finding: Limits and inferences stated by the authors: the cause or causes of EVALI are unknown; VEA is high-molecular-mass, lipophilic and similar to oils known to cause lipoid pneumonia, so it is possible that it is causative or contributes; initial experiments (not shown) indicate compounds including duroquinone form when VEA is vaped; extensive in vitro and in vivo studies are required to establish cause.

Funding: none external. Declared conflicts: none. Authors are employees of the New York State Department of Health Wadsworth Center and Center for Environmental Health, with academic affiliations at the University at Albany and Albany Medical Center.
key_findings.locator: Funding; Conflicts of Interest; author affiliations

reporting_issues.issue: The text says MCT oil was detected in 15 fluids; Table 1 marks 14 fluids with a plus sign (samples 3, 7, 14, 15, 18, 24, 26, 28, 29, 30, 31, 32, 33 and 34).
reporting_issues.consequence: Which fluid is the fifteenth is not clear, and the 3 to 24% range cannot be checked because per-sample MCT amounts are not tabulated.

reporting_issues.issue: The basis for calling the cartridges illicit is not stated. The title, abstract and Discussion say illicit or street products; the Methods say only that case-associated cartridges were collected and that packaging and markings were noted.
reporting_issues.consequence: The label may be an inference from the contents, the cartridges' look or the patients' accounts; the shares cannot be applied to 'illicit' cartridges as a class.

reporting_issues.issue: The extended series (206 fluids from 61 cases; 101 of 147 with VEA) appears only in the Conclusions, with no methods, no table and no statement of whether the first 38 are included.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 69% cannot be checked and overlaps the 64% from the first 10 cases; the two should not be counted as independent.

reporting_issues.issue: The upper VEA value is given as 57% in the Results, 57.6% in Table 1 and 58% in the Discussion; Table 1 units are not printed in the text read.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results 3.2, 3rd paragraph; Table 1; Discussion 4.1
reporting_issues.consequence: Rounding only; the units are inferred from the surrounding text.

reporting_issues.issue: Results are not given per patient: the 38 fluids are listed by sample number only.
reporting_issues.consequence: It cannot be seen how many of the 10 patients had a VEA-containing cartridge, or whether the 13 fluids without VEA came from patients who also had one that did.

reporting_issues.issue: Claims that the lab's medical-program products are 80 to 90% cannabinoids and free of additives, that heating VEA forms compounds including duroquinone, and that the extended series found more VEA are given without data.
reporting_issues.consequence: These statements are the authors' account and are not checkable from the paper.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC7151740 (all sections, Tables 1 to 3, figure captions, funding and conflict statements, author affiliations and reference list read as text; Figures 1 to 5 were not viewed as images; the supplementary PDF with Figures S1 to S6 and Table S1 was not opened)
